references.text: Pigs were considered unclean animals according to the Mosaic Law ([ref:3 Mos 11:7-8|Leviticus 11:7-8]). The fact that the prodigal son was sent to tend pigs shows how far he had fallen – he served a Gentile and worked with what was most unclean for a Jew.
The pig is mentioned among the unclean animals in [ref:5 Mos 14:8|Deuteronomy 14:8], which underscores the deep degradation the prodigal son experienced by tending pigs.

The curse in [ref:5 Mos 28:48|Deuteronomy 28:48] describes serving enemies in hunger and distress, a situation reflected in the prodigal son's plight as he had to serve a foreigner in deep humiliation.

In [ref:Jes 65:4|Isaiah 65:4], those who eat pork and linger among graves are condemned. For a Jew, tending pigs was the ultimate symbol of apostasy and uncleanness – exactly where the prodigal son had sunk.

The verb "ἐκολλήθη" (clung to / attached himself) is also used in [ref:Apg 9:26|Acts 9:26], where Paul tried to "join" the disciples. In Luke 15:15, the word carries a desperate tone – the prodigal son clung to a foreign citizen to survive.

The context in [ref:Luk 15:13-14|Luke 15:13-14] shows that the prodigal son had squandered everything he owned and was in distress when a famine came. This forced him into the desperate act of seeking work from a Gentile as a swineherd.

The following verse [ref:Luk 15:16|Luke 15:16] further elaborates on his humiliation: he longed to fill his stomach with what the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything. Together with verse 15, this paints a picture of deepest need and degradation.
